Cell.Data: A phishing or look-alike chat UI harvests the user's password and TOTP code; the attacker then signs in as that user.
Collect credentials only on Auth0 Universal Login. Enforce TOTP MFA, brute-force protection and Suspicious IP Throttling. Use a custom domain and train users.
XSS or a malicious browser extension changes chat input, or submits injected prompts in the user's name.
Strict CSP with no inline script, Subresource Integrity, output encoding and Trusted Types.
A user denies typing a harmful prompt that triggered an agent action.
Attribution captured server-side on F04 (user sub, session ID, prompt hash, timestamp).
Tokens kept in localStorage, or chat content left on a shared device, can be read by XSS or the next user.
Backend-for-frontend: tokens stay server-side, HttpOnly cookies, idle auto-logout, nothing sensitive in browser storage.
N/A: the interaction stays on the user's own device, with no shared resource to exhaust. Service-level DoS is covered on F02 and F04.
N/A: no privilege boundary is crossed; the user acts only with their own rights. Privilege checks happen at F04, F05 and F08.
Login CSRF or callback injection: an attacker's authorization code is injected into the victim's browser, or an open redirect sends the code to an attacker URL.
Exact-match Allowed Callback URLs, state and nonce checks, HTTPS only, no wildcard redirect URIs.
Authorization request tampering: code_challenge removed (PKCE downgrade), redirect_uri changed, or write:admin added to scope.
Require PKCE S256. Scopes granted by Auth0 RBAC, not the client request; write:admin issued only to the admin role.
A user disputes a login or MFA event.
Stream Auth0 tenant logs (login success/failure, MFA enrol/challenge) to the SIEM with retention.
The authorization code leaks through Referer, browser history or proxy logs.
Single-use, short-lived codes; PKCE makes a leaked code useless without the verifier; Referrer-Policy no-referrer; response_mode=form_post.
Credential stuffing or login floods lock out legitimate users and exhaust Auth0 rate limits.
Brute-force protection (10 attempts, 15-minute block), Suspicious IP Throttling and Bot Detection.
MFA is bypassed, or a self-signup / account-linking path grants elevated roles.
Enforce MFA for all users. Restrict public signup so new users get only the user role. Admin roles assigned only by tenant admins.
The backend accepts a forged token (alg=none, HS256/RS256 key confusion) or a token issued for another tenant or audience.
Verify RS256 against the Auth0 JWKS, pin the algorithm, check iss, aud, exp, nbf and the ID-token nonce.
JWT claims (scope, agent_id, roles) are edited to gain access.
Use claims only after signature verification; reject unsigned tokens and unknown kid values.
There is no way to prove which token was issued to which session or client.
Correlate Auth0 seacft (code exchange) logs with backend logs by sub, client_id, jti and session ID.
The client secret or tokens are written to application logs, or the ID token over-shares PII.
Client secret in Secrets Manager; scrub Authorization headers and tokens from logs; minimal claims; TLS 1.2+.
An Auth0 outage, rate limiting or a failed JWKS fetch blocks every login and token validation.
Cache JWKS with refresh on unknown kid; retry with exponential backoff; fail closed with a clear error.
The backend accepts an ID token as an API access token, or long-lived tokens extend the attack window.
APIs accept only access tokens with the correct aud; access-token TTL 300 s; refresh-token rotation with reuse detection.
Session hijacking with a stolen cookie, or CSRF sends chat requests as the victim.
Cookies HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict; anti-CSRF token; session rotation at login; short idle and absolute timeouts.
The client injects role or user_id fields into the request body, or embeds a direct prompt injection.
Take identity only from the server-side session and ignore client identity fields; schema validation; input guardrails.
A user denies sending the prompt that led to an agent action.
Tamper-evident audit log of sub, session ID, request ID, prompt hash and timestamp.
IDOR on a conversation ID exposes another user's chat, or verbose errors or model output leak secrets.
Conversation ownership check; generic errors; output guardrail that redacts JWT-shaped strings.
Prompt flooding or oversized prompts burn the LLM budget (denial of wallet).
Per-user rate limits, maximum input tokens, WAF, request body size limits.
A user-level session reaches admin functions through hidden endpoints, or by asking the agent to act as admin.
Server-side RBAC (read:ai-data vs write:admin) returns 403; the agent never gets more privilege than the calling user.
An attacker skips the backend and calls the harness directly with a forged user context.
Network policy so only the backend can reach the harness; mutual TLS or an Ed25519-signed context envelope verified by the harness.
User context (sub, roles) is changed in transit, or user text mixed into the prompt overrides the system instructions.
Send user context as signed structured metadata, separate from the prompt; immutable system prompt; input guardrails.
Agent actions cannot be traced back to the originating user (confused-deputy audit gap).
Pass request ID, user sub and agent_id to every downstream call and log them at each hop.
The system prompt, or credentials embedded in it, is extracted and returned to the user (LLM07).
No secrets in the system prompt; output guardrail; canary strings to detect leakage.
Agent reasoning or tool-call loops use up compute and tokens.
Maximum agent steps, per-request timeout, token budget per conversation.
The agent acts with its own M2M privileges instead of the user's, so users gain indirect access (confused deputy).
Authorize downstream actions against the intersection of user and agent scope, using token exchange / on-behalf-of with an act claim.
Another service connects with shared database credentials and poses as the backend.
Per-service DB identity (IAM authentication), network ACLs, no shared DB accounts.
Stored chat history is edited to plant a persistent prompt injection (memory poisoning).
Backend-only write access, parameterized queries, history treated as untrusted when re-prompting, integrity hash on records.
Chat history is deleted or changed without a trace.
DB audit logging and an append-only audit table.
A DB breach or backup leak exposes transcripts that contain PII or tokens.
Encryption at rest, redact tokens before writing, retention limits, per-user row-level access.
Very large transcripts or abusive volume exhaust storage.
Message size caps, per-user quotas, retention and purge jobs.
SQL injection through chat content gives DB admin rights.
Parameterized queries and a least-privilege DB role (DML only, no DDL).
Another workload impersonates the harness to read its secrets.
Workload identity (cloud IAM role / SPIFFE), with each secret's access policy bound to the harness identity only.
A secret is replaced with an attacker-controlled value, for example to route LLM traffic to the attacker's account.
Restrict write access, version secrets, alert on every secret change.
No record of who read or rotated a secret.
Send Secrets Manager access logs to the SIEM.
The LLM API key or M2M secret is loaded into env vars or prompt context and exfiltrated through prompt injection (Attack Tree 1).
Never put secrets in model context (HTTP client only); short-lived M2M tokens; rotate keys at least every 90 days; redact output.
If Secrets Manager is unavailable, the agent cannot authenticate.
In-memory cache with a TTL, highly available secrets service, alerting.
The harness has wildcard read access to every secret, so one compromise exposes all credentials.
Least-privilege policy per secret path, reviewed quarterly.
AI Chatbot Harness → Internal REST APIs
A stolen M2M token or client secret lets an attacker pose as the agent (Attack Tree 2).
TTL 60-300 s; private_key_jwt or mTLS sender-constrained tokens; source-IP allow-list; alert on token reuse after expiry.
AI Chatbot Harness → Internal REST APIs
A prompt-injected agent changes API parameters, for example the customer ID or amount.
Server-side per-object authorization against the propagated user context; strict parameter validation.
AI Chatbot Harness → Internal REST APIs
The API cannot tell whether the agent acted for user A or user B.
Log client_id, agent_id, user sub (act claim), scope and request ID on every call.
AI Chatbot Harness → Internal REST APIs
The API returns more data than needed, and that data then flows into the LLM.
Field-level filtering, data minimization, scope-based response shaping.
AI Chatbot Harness → Internal REST APIs
A spike in agent call volume overwhelms internal APIs.
Per-client rate limits; alert when there are more than 20 requests in 60 s.
AI Chatbot Harness → Internal REST APIs
The agent's M2M client has write:admin, or its scope changes between consecutive requests.
Grant the M2M client only the scopes it needs, enforce scope at the API, alert on scope change.
A DNS or proxy misconfiguration sends prompts to a fake LLM endpoint, or a stolen key lets someone pose as SecureNova to the provider.
TLS certificate validation, fixed provider hostname, egress allow-list, provider-side key restrictions.
A man-in-the-middle changes model responses in transit.
TLS 1.2+; treat model output as untrusted; validate every proposed tool call.
LLM usage and cost cannot be attributed to a user or agent.
Separate keys per environment, request IDs and user tags in provider metadata, usage logs in the SIEM.
Prompts send PII, tokens or the system prompt to a third party, which may retain them.
Minimize and redact data before sending; zero-retention agreement / DPA with the provider.
Abuse exhausts the provider's rate limit or quota (denial of wallet).
Spend budgets and quotas, circuit breaker, fallback model.
Model output tells the harness to call privileged tools or APIs (excessive agency, LLM06).
Tool allow-list per user role, policy engine outside the LLM, human approval for privileged actions.
An unauthenticated caller queries the RAG service directly, or the harness claims a different user to get their documents.
RAG requires an agent workload token; per-user ACL filters come only from the verified context.
Queries are crafted to pull poisoned chunks, or retrieved text is changed in transit.
TLS, provenance-tagged and hash-verified chunks, content sanitization.
No record of which chunks shaped an answer or action.
Log chunk ID, source document and version for every request.
Semantic search leaks documents across users or tenants.
Enforce document-level ACLs at retrieval with metadata filters, never only in the prompt.
Expensive queries (large top-k, long text) slow the service down.
Cap top-k and query length; timeouts and rate limits.
A retrieved chunk carries instructions the agent follows to escalate its actions (indirect prompt injection, Attack Tree 3).
Treat chunks as data (spotlighting/delimiters); input guardrails on retrieved text; privileged actions need authorization outside the LLM.
A rogue embedding endpoint is substituted for the real one.
Fixed endpoint configuration; mTLS or API-key auth between services.
Embedding vectors or the model version are manipulated to steer retrieval.
Pin the model version, integrity-checked deployments, TLS.
Nobody can tell which embedding model version indexed a chunk.
Record the embedding model ID and version with every indexed chunk.
Document text is sent to a third-party embedding API.
Self-hosted or approved provider; redact sensitive fields before embedding.
An embedding service outage blocks both retrieval and ingestion.
Retries, a query-embedding cache, a queue for ingestion.
N/A: the embedding service is a stateless transform that only returns vectors. It makes no authorization decisions and has no privileged operations.
An unauthorized writer poses as the ingestion pipeline and inserts chunks.
Separate identities for querying (read) and ingestion (write), with authentication enforced on the vector DB.
Chunk poisoning: malicious instructions are inserted or edited in the store (Attack Tree 3).
Ingestion review and content scanning, signed chunk hashes checked at retrieval, provenance metadata.
No one can tell who inserted or changed a chunk.
Store author, source and ingest time on each chunk, with audit logs on writes.
The vector store is exposed, or embeddings are inverted to reconstruct the source text.
Private network, authentication, encryption at rest.
The index is deleted or corrupted.
Snapshots and backups, restricted delete rights, tested restore.
The RAG query identity has write or admin rights on the store.
Read-only role for the query path; only the ingestion identity can write.
A rogue or look-alike MCP server or tool is registered (tool shadowing), or a caller poses as the agent to the MCP server.
MCP server allow-list with a pinned identity (mTLS/OAuth); the agent authenticates with a signed, audience-bound token.
A tool manifest or description is poisoned, or injected content changes tool arguments.
Pin and hash tool manifests, validate arguments against a JSON schema, Ed25519-sign agent messages.
A tool invocation cannot be traced to the agent or user who triggered it.
Log tool name, argument hash, agent_id, user sub, request ID and result.
Tool results containing secrets go back into the LLM context, or the MCP server logs tokens.
Filter and redact tool results; never pass tokens through.
Long-running or hanging tools block the agent.
A poisoned chunk triggers a privileged MCP tool, such as a refund or delete.
Per-tool scopes, deny by default, human-in-the-loop approval for destructive tools.
The MCP server uses a shared or static credential, which an attacker steals to pose as the MCP server.
Dedicated M2M client for the MCP server, with short-TTL, sender-constrained tokens.
The MCP server rewrites requests beyond what the agent asked for.
The API validates each request against the propagated user and agent context; requests are signed.
API logs show only the MCP identity, so the user → agent → tool chain is lost.
Pass the actor chain (RFC 8693 act claim) and request ID, and log them at the API.
The API returns more data than the MCP tool needs.
A storm of tool calls overloads internal APIs.
Rate limits per MCP client, plus a circuit breaker.
Token passthrough: the MCP server forwards the agent's token, or uses its own broader rights (confused deputy).
No token passthrough; the MCP server gets an audience-specific token through token exchange, with scopes no wider than the caller's.
STRIDE coverage summary (live formulas over the STRIDE Matrix sheet)
Credential or token compromise, privilege escalation, cross-user data exposure, or loss of attribution for privileged actions.
Limited data exposure, integrity loss without direct privilege gain, or availability or cost impact.
Minor or hard-to-exploit impact. Numeric Likelihood x Impact scoring is done in the attack trees and risk register.

Task-required boundaries: user layer → agent layer = TB1 → TB3/TB4 (F04, F05); agent layer → internal API layer = TB4 → TB5 (F08) and TB4 → TB7 → TB5 (F13, F14).
